1198.title: The Talk in Ayodhya
1198.word: each as a lens for a week
1198.hook: Rama hears what the city is saying about Sita: Nyaya asks whose word it is, Vaisheshika asks what you're looking at
1198.carry: nyaya: knowing needs a reliable word, not a rumor
1198.tomorrow: a mother asks her son how to be free.
1198.howItsDone: Nyaya and Vaisheshika are traditionally studied together, and students of Indian logic learn the Nyaya Sutra's means of knowing, including the rule that word counts only from a reliable person, alongside Vaisheshika's categories of what there is.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna's new eyes: darshana, to see and be seen; six ways of seeing. Today, the first pair, through one of the hardest chapters in the Ramayana.
screen: `SIX WAYS OF SEEING.` · `THE FIRST PAIR.`

segments.voice: Rama is home. The war is won, Sita is back, and Ayodhya has its king. In the last book of Valmiki's Ramayana, Rama asks a courtier named Bhadra what people in the city are saying. Bhadra hesitates, then tells him. They praise the war. But they talk about Sita: she lived in Ravana's palace, and the king took her back. Later tellings put the words in the mouth of a washerman scolding his own wife. Either way, it's talk. And the king acts on it. Sita, carrying his children, is taken to the forest and left there. Hindus have argued about this chapter for centuries. Today's first pair of lenses shows one way to see why it hurts.
screen: `WHAT IS THE CITY SAYING?` → `TALK ABOUT SITA.` → `THE KING ACTS ON IT.`

segments.voice: First, the Nyaya lens. Its question: how do I know? The Nyaya Sutra names the means of right knowing: perception, inference, comparison, and word. And word counts only when it comes from a reliable person, someone who knows the matter and tells it straight. Click that lens onto Ayodhya. What did the city see? Nothing; they weren't in Lanka. What's left is talk, passed hand to hand by people who don't know. Under Nyaya, that isn't knowledge. It isn't even false yet. It's simply not known. And there was reliable word on the other side: Sita's own, and the fire she walked into in Lanka, which, the Ramayana says, gave her back unharmed. Now the Vaisheshika lens. Its question: what is this made of? Kanada's school sorts the world into categories: substance, quality, action, and more. Many teachers use it this way: a thing isn't the same as one act done around it. The city's talk is the city's act, not a quality of Sita. That's the teaching under today: in Hindu thought, knowing is something you check, not something you catch. Pramana, the means of knowing, has to hold. The playwright Bhavabhuti built a whole play around Rama's grief over this choice; others read it as a king bound to his people's trust. Either way, the two lenses won't let talk pass for knowledge just because it's loud.
screen: `NYAYA: HOW DO I KNOW?` · `WHOSE WORD IS IT?` · `VAISHESHIKA: WHAT IS THIS MADE OF?` · `TALK IS NOT KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you heard lately about a person you know, and ask the Nyaya question: did I see this, reason to it, or hear it, and if I heard it, does the one who said it really know? Then the Vaisheshika question: is this the person, one act of theirs, or only talk about them? Let what isn't known yet stay not known. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer; if you don't, simply wish them well.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the first pair: Nyaya asks how do I know, Vaisheshika asks what is this made of. Today's word.

1199.title: Kapila Teaches His Mother
1199.word: each as a lens for a week
1199.hook: Devahuti, worn out by wanting, asks her son Kapila how to be free: the second pair of lenses, Samkhya and Yoga
1199.carry: samkhya and yoga: the seer is not the storm
1199.tomorrow: a great debate, and two garlands.
1199.howItsDone: Samkhya and Yoga are traditionally studied as a pair, and many Hindus first meet Samkhya's ideas in the Bhagavata, where Kapila teaches his mother Devahuti; the Yoga Sutra is the guide many use for stilling the mind.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Ayodhya, nyaya: knowing needs a reliable word, not a rumor. Today, the second pair.
screen: `A RELIABLE WORD, NOT A RUMOR.` · `THE SECOND PAIR.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata's third book, Devahuti has lived a long, full life. Her husband, the sage Kardama, has gone off to the forest. Her son stays with her. His name is Kapila, and tradition remembers a sage named Kapila as the founder of Samkhya. One day she comes to him and says, in effect: I'm worn out by the cravings of my senses. I've been lost in a darkness that won't lift. You've come to be my light. Teach me how to be free. A son becomes his mother's teacher, and what he teaches is the second pair: Samkhya and Yoga.
screen: `A MOTHER, WORN OUT BY WANTING.` → `HER SON, KAPILA.` → `TEACH ME HOW TO BE FREE.`

segments.voice: Kapila starts with the Samkhya question: who is watching? He draws the great division. On one side, prakriti, nature: everything that moves and changes, the body, the senses, even the mind and the sense of I. On the other, purusha, the self, who sees and doesn't act. The trouble, he tells her, is that the self takes nature's movements as its own. Nature does the doing, and the self thinks: I am doing this, I am suffering this. Then comes a line the Bhagavata is known for: the mind is the cause of bondage, and the mind is the cause of freedom. Tied to the world's pulls, it binds. Turned toward the Lord, it frees. The Bhagavata's Kapila is a devotee as well as a philosopher; the classic Samkhya texts don't speak of God this way. Now the Yoga lens. Its question: what is the mind doing right now? Patanjali's Yoga Sutra defines yoga as the stilling of the mind's movements. Then the seer rests in its own nature; otherwise it seems to take the mind's shapes. How do the movements settle? By practice and by letting go. That's the teaching under these two: in Hindu thought, you are not your passing states. Anger, fear, a speech building in your head: all of it is nature moving. The one who sees it isn't burning. Devahuti, the Bhagavata says, practiced what her son taught her, and reached freedom.
screen: `SAMKHYA: WHO IS WATCHING?` · `THE MIND BINDS, THE MIND FREES.` · `YOGA: STILLING THE MIND.` · `YOU ARE NOT YOUR PASSING STATES.`

segments.voice: Let a recent flash of anger or worry come to mind. With the Samkhya lens, notice that all of it, the heat, the story, even the I that was hurt, is being seen, and rest a few breaths as the one who sees. With the Yoga lens, come back to your breath, stay a little longer than is easy, and loosen your grip on how it should have gone. If you pray, turn that mind toward the One you pray to, as Kapila told his mother; if you don't, simply let it settle.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the second pair: Samkhya asks who is watching, Yoga asks what the mind is doing. Today's word.

1200.title: The Debate and the Two Garlands
1200.word: each as a lens for a week
1200.hook: Shankara comes to debate Mandana Mishra, and Mandana's wife holds the garlands: the last pair, Mimamsa and Vedanta, and a verse Hindus say before meals
1200.carry: brahmarpanam: every act, even a meal, offered to brahman
1200.tomorrow: a scholar forgets his wife, then names a book for her.
1200.howItsDone: Mimamsa and Vedanta are traditionally studied as the earlier and later inquiry, and many Hindu families recite Bhagavad Gita 4.24, which begins brahmarpanam, before a meal.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line, samkhya and yoga: the seer is not the storm. Kapila taught it to his mother. Today, the last pair.
screen: `THE SEER IS NOT THE STORM.` · `THE LAST PAIR.`

segments.voice: This one comes from a later life of Shankara, so hold it as legend. The young teacher of Vedanta walks into the town of Mahishmati, looking for the greatest scholar of Mimamsa, Mandana Mishra. How will he find the house? Look for the one, people tell him, where even the parrots at the door argue about whether the Veda stands on its own authority. The two men debate for days. The judge is Mandana's own wife, Ubhaya Bharati, a scholar herself. She puts a fresh garland around each man's neck. Whoever's garland wilts first, she says, has lost. Ritual against knowledge: the last pair of lenses.
screen: `LOOKING FOR MANDANA MISHRA.` → `PARROTS AT THE DOOR.` → `THE JUDGE AND TWO GARLANDS.`

segments.voice: Mandana's school is Mimamsa. Its question: what is this act for? Mimamsa reads the Veda as a book of things to do: rites done rightly, in order, many of them daily. Shankara's school is Vedanta. Its question: what does all of it rest on? For Shankara, rites purify the heart, but freedom comes from knowing Brahman, the one reality under everything. In the legend, Mandana's garland fades first, and he becomes Shankara's student. But Mimamsa didn't vanish. Hindu homes still keep daily rites, and priests still ask how a rite is done rightly. And one verse holds both lenses. Many Hindu families say it before they eat. It's from the Bhagavad Gita, chapter four. In paraphrase: the offering is Brahman. The food offered is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. The one who sees Brahman in every act reaches Brahman. Mimamsa recognizes every piece: an offering, a fire, the one who offers. Vedanta sees what each piece rests on. That's the teaching under today. In Hinduism, an ordinary act, even eating, can be an offering. Many teachers read the verse at the table this way: the plate is the offering, the hunger is the fire, and the eater is the one who offers. None of it is outside Brahman. Some families say it aloud; some just fold their hands. Either way, dinner stops being just fuel.
screen: `WHAT IT'S FOR, WHAT IT RESTS ON.` · `ONE VERSE HOLDS BOTH LENSES.` · `THE OFFERING IS BRAHMAN.` · `A MEAL CAN BE AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, or right now with a glass of water, pause before the first bite or sip. Families who say the verse begin with one word, brahmarpanam, the offering is Brahman. You can say that word, or simply look at the food, the hand and the hunger, and see them as one offering. If you pray, offer the meal to the One you pray to; if you don't, take the first bite in full thanks.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the third pair: Mimamsa asks what this act is for, Vedanta asks what it all rests on. Today's word.

1201.title: The Book Named for His Wife
1201.word: each as a lens for a week
1201.hook: a story people tell about a scholar who wrote careful books on schools that disagreed, and named one of them after his wife
1201.carry: one truth, six darshanas: lenses, not team jerseys
1201.tomorrow: Krishna is leaving, and his friend asks to come.
1201.howItsDone: Traditional students of Indian philosophy learn the darshanas from their own root texts and commentaries, and classical scholars such as Vachaspati Mishra wrote commentaries on several schools, setting out each one's case in its own terms.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, two garlands, Mimamsa and Vedanta, and brahmarpanam: every act, even a meal, offered to Brahman.
screen: `THE LAST PAIR.` · `ALL SIX, ONE SHELF.`

segments.voice: There's a story people tell about a scholar named Vachaspati Mishra. He was writing a commentary, and he worked at it so long and so completely that he lost track of everything else, including the woman who kept the lamp lit beside him, his wife. When he finally looked up and asked who she was, she told him. Moved, so the story goes, he named the book after her: the Bhamati. The story may be legend. But the scholar's shelf is real, and it's strange. On the last day of this part, it shows how to hold all six darshanas at once.
screen: `A SCHOLAR BENT OVER HIS BOOK.` → `THE ONE WHO KEPT THE LAMP LIT.` → `A BOOK NAMED FOR HER.`

segments.voice: Here's what's strange about the shelf. The Bhamati is a Vedanta commentary, in Shankara's line. But Vachaspati Mishra is also remembered for commentaries on Nyaya, on Samkhya, on Yoga and on Mimamsa. Schools that argue with each other, sometimes sharply. Among them, a commentary on a book by Mandana Mishra, yesterday's debater. And he wrote on each of them from the inside, carefully, laying out its case in its own terms. That's what a lens is. Not a team jersey. A way of seeing you learn well enough to look through. So here are all six, one last time. Nyaya: how do I know? Vaisheshika: what is this made of? Samkhya: who is watching? Yoga: what is the mind doing? Mimamsa: what is this act for? Vedanta: what does all of it rest on? Why can one tradition hold all six? Many Hindus reach for a line from the Rig Veda: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. It's about the names of the divine, but many teachers read it as the spirit of the six schools too. That's the teaching to keep: in Hinduism, a darshana is a way of seeing, and one truth can be seen from more than one side. It ends with no winner. That's the point of the part we're closing, schools of thought, never ranked. The tradition kept all six on one shelf, argued among them for a long time, and kept the lamp lit for the next reader. Tomorrow the lineage track picks up again, with a different teacher, Krishna speaking to his friend Uddhava in the Bhagavata, on action.
screen: `ONE SCHOLAR, MANY SCHOOLS.` · `A LENS, NOT A TEAM JERSEY.` · `TRUTH IS ONE; MANY NAMES.` · `SIX WAYS OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Picture the first ordinary thing you'll do tomorrow morning, filling a kettle, finding your keys, opening a door, and let whichever of the six questions arrives first stand in front of it. Look through it for a few breaths and notice what comes into focus, then set the lens down and rest in the plain scene without any question at all. If you pray, you can ask for clear sight.
Each as a lens for a week. The six darshanas, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta, each tried for a day, none of them ranked. Today's word.

1202.title: Take Me With You
1202.hook: Krishna is about to leave the world, and his friend asks for one thing: take me with you
1202.carry: karma: keep acting, with your mind on krishna
1202.tomorrow: a king asks a wanderer where his calm comes from.
1202.howItsDone: Students of the Bhagavata Purana read the eleventh book's long dialogue between Krishna and Uddhava, known as the Uddhava Gita, as a teaching in its own right, and it is recited along with the rest of the Purana when the whole text is read aloud.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Last week ended on one truth, six darshanas: lenses, not team jerseys. Now the lineage track comes back, on the path of action.
screen: `SIX LENSES, NONE RANKED.` · `NOW, THE PATH OF ACTION.`

segments.voice: Krishna is about to leave the world. In the Bhagavata's eleventh book, the gods come to remind him that his work on earth is done, and his own clan is heading toward its end. Uddhava hears it: his close friend, the learned messenger who once carried his words to Vraja. He comes to Krishna alone and asks for one thing: take me with you. He says he can't bear to be apart from him. What Krishna gives him instead is a long teaching. Tradition calls it the Uddhava Gita.
screen: `KRISHNA IS ABOUT TO LEAVE.` → `TAKE ME WITH YOU.` → `WHAT HE GETS INSTEAD: A TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Krishna's first answer sounds hard. Don't follow me, he says. When I'm gone, let go of your attachment to family and friends, fix your mind on me, and wander the earth seeing everything evenly. Uddhava doesn't pretend. In effect he says: this kind of letting go is hard for people like me, whose minds cling to the body and to what is ours. Teach me how. And Krishna does, chapter after chapter, before he goes. That's the shape of the whole Uddhava Gita: an honest question, and a teacher who stays to answer it. Why read it on the path of action? Back on day seven, karma meant action itself, not payback. And Uddhava isn't a sage in a cave. He's a man with duties, a household, a city, and a friend about to be gone. His question is the karma question: how do I keep acting in a world that keeps losing things? The next few days come at it from several sides: what to learn from the people who wrong you, which path suits whom, where joy and sorrow really come from, and how to work without hurry. And notice: Krishna doesn't take Uddhava with him. The teacher leaves, and the student keeps living. That's the teaching under the whole book, karma yoga in Krishna's last words: keep acting in the world, with your mind fixed on God, even after the one you leaned on is gone.
screen: `DON'T FOLLOW ME. LET GO, AND WANDER.` · `THIS IS HARD FOR ME. TEACH ME HOW.` · `THE KARMA QUESTION: HOW DO I KEEP ACTING?` · `KEEP ACTING, MIND ON KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something and isn't here to ask anymore, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who moved away, and instead of reaching for the loss, reach for one thing they left you: a habit, a saying, a way of doing an ordinary job. Hold that one thing, and if you pray, offer that person and that gift to the One you pray to. If a loss feels too heavy to hold alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
Karma. Action, work, the deed itself. In the Uddhava Gita it begins with one honest question: how to keep acting when the one you leaned on is leaving.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma, keep acting, with your mind on Krishna. What the teacher left is what you work with now. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1203.title: The Wanderer and the Earth
1203.hook: a king meets a young wanderer with nothing, and asks where his calm comes from
1203.carry: the earth is a guru: pushed, it doesn't swerve
1203.tomorrow: who is the path of action really for?
1203.howItsDone: The avadhuta's list of teachers in the Bhagavata's eleventh book is a familiar teaching story among Hindus, and tradition identifies the avadhuta with Dattatreya, honored as a teacher of teachers.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma began with a goodbye: Uddhava asked to be taken along, and Krishna stayed to teach him instead.
screen: `TAKE ME WITH YOU.` · `A TEACHING INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: A king out in the world meets a young man who owns nothing. No house, no plans, no worry on his face. The king is Yadu, an ancestor of Krishna's own clan, and he can't help asking. You're clever and capable, he says, yet you live like a child, untroubled. People all around are burning with wanting, and you stand there cool, like an elephant in a river while the forest burns. Where does your calm come from? Krishna tells this story to Uddhava early in their dialogue. The wanderer is an avadhuta, one who lives outside the world's usual rules. His answer: I've had many teachers. And the first one is right under your feet.
screen: `A KING MEETS A WANDERER.` → `WHERE DOES YOUR CALM COME FROM?` → `I'VE HAD MANY TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: The first teacher is the earth. In paraphrase, here's what the avadhuta learned from it: a steady person, even when pushed around by other beings, remembers that they too are moved by forces beyond their control, and doesn't step off the path. People dig the earth, plow it, build on it and walk on it all day. It doesn't shake anyone off. It keeps holding things up and growing food. This is karma from an unexpected side. Karma talk often starts with my actions and what comes back to me. The avadhuta turns it around. The other person, the one acting badly, is caught in a web of causes too. Not excused. Understood. Their action is theirs; my steadiness is mine. And the earth doesn't pretend nothing happened, or argue. It simply doesn't swerve. That isn't being a doormat. It's not letting someone else's bad day rewrite your path. After the earth come twenty-three more: the wind, the sky, water, fire, the moon, a python, a moth, a honeybee and others. Tradition identifies the wanderer with Dattatreya, and many Hindus know this list as his twenty-four gurus. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, a guru can be anything you learn from, and the world itself is a classroom. The list begins at the ground, with the teacher everybody stands on.
screen: `THE EARTH: PUSHED, AND STILL STEADY.` · `OTHERS ARE MOVED BY CAUSES TOO.` · `NOT A DOORMAT: JUST DON'T SWERVE.` · `TWENTY-FOUR GURUS.`

segments.voice: Feel what's holding you up, the chair, the floor, the earth under the building, and let your weight go into it. Bring to mind one person who pushed you lately with a sharp word or a careless move, and without replaying it, say to yourself: they were moved by things I can't see; then come back to the ground holding you. If you pray, you can hold that person before the One you pray to.
Karma. Action, and the web of causes behind it. From the earth the avadhuta learned that others are moved by causes too, and not to swerve.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the earth is a guru, pushed, it doesn't swerve. The ground takes every step and still holds. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1203 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO IS THE PATH OF ACTION REALLY FOR?`

1204.title: Three Paths, Three Kinds of People
1204.hook: who is the path of action actually for? the Uddhava Gita answers: people who still want things
1204.carry: karma yoga: the path for hearts that still want
1204.tomorrow: a miser loses everything, and sings.
1204.howItsDone: Hindu teachers speak of three paths, jnana, karma and bhakti, and some say a student's temperament and stage of life help decide which path to emphasize, drawing on teachings like this one in the Bhagavata's eleventh book.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's karma came from the ground: the earth is a guru, pushed all day, and it doesn't swerve.
screen: `THE EARTH DOESN'T SWERVE.` · `WHO IS ACTION FOR?`

segments.voice: Who is the path of action actually for? Deep in the dialogue, Uddhava asks something close to it. The Vedas, he says in effect, tell people what to do and what not to do. They praise good works, and they also speak of a state beyond works altogether. So which is it? Do something, or stop doing? It sounds like a question that needs a side. Krishna doesn't pick one. He looks at the people asking, and sorts the paths by who's walking them.
screen: `DO SOMETHING, OR STOP DOING?` → `KRISHNA DOESN'T PICK A SIDE.` → `HE LOOKS AT THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Krishna says he has given three yogas, three paths, so people can reach the good: jnana, the path of knowing; karma, the path of action; and bhakti, the path of devotion. Then the sorting. Jnana suits those who have grown weary of action and turned away from it. Karma suits those who haven't, whose hearts still hold desires, who still want things from the world. And bhakti suits someone who, by some good fortune, has come to love hearing about him, neither fed up with the world nor tied too tightly to it. Sit with that middle line. The path of action isn't reserved for finished saints. It's for people with ambitions, a to-do list, a pull toward the world. The Uddhava Gita doesn't scold that wanting. It gives it a road. How long does a person stay on it? The very next verse answers: keep doing the work until you grow weary of it, or until faith in hearing his stories wakes up. Two ways off the road, and no deadline. For someone in the middle of a busy life, it's a quietly kind teaching. It doesn't say drop everything first, then you can begin. It says begin where your wanting already is.
screen: `THREE PATHS: KNOWING, ACTION, LOVE.` · `ACTION IS FOR THOSE WHO STILL WANT.` · `STAY UNTIL WEARY, OR UNTIL FAITH WAKES.` · `BEGIN WHERE YOUR WANTING IS.`

segments.voice: Without judging it, let one thing you want rise up, a result at work, a change at home, something you're building, and look at it clearly, the way you'd look at a road from the top of a hill. Then ask what one honest piece of work this wanting is asking of you. If you pray, you can offer that wanting, just as it is, to the One you pray to.
Karma. In the Uddhava Gita, the path of action: for hearts that still want things, walked until weariness comes or faith wakes up.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma yoga, the path for hearts that still want. Begin where your wanting is. Same time tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1204 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A MISER LOSES EVERYTHING, AND SINGS.`
